title: Rain-day school bag
prompt: Monsoon in Kerala: a child walks 2 km to school in heavy rain carrying books, a tiffin box and a water bottle. Sketch three different ideas to keep books and the child dry and comfortable. Each idea must work differently (not three versions of a raincoat). Label each sketch in one or two lines and circle the idea you would develop.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Number and variety of genuinely different ideas
Fit to the situation (rain, walking distance, load)
Reasoned choice of the best idea

tips: Change the principle (cover, container, route, material) rather than the shape.
Show how the child uses it with a small figure.
Spend the last 3 minutes on the choice and one line of reasoning.

title: Sharing one mobile phone
prompt: In many homes one smartphone is shared by three or four family members. Suggest four small product or object ideas that make sharing easier, fairer or safer. Draw each as a quick thumbnail with a short caption stating the problem it solves.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet
tips: Think about time, privacy, charging and storage as separate problems.
Keep thumbnails small so you have time for all four.

title: A story in four frames
prompt: Tell a wordless story in exactly four frames drawn on one A4 sheet: a lantern seller at a night fair gets his last lantern and a lost child comes to him. The last frame must show an unexpected but warm ending. Use no more than five words of text in total.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Clear beginning, turn and ending across four frames
Character and emotion shown through drawing
Composition and variation of viewpoint between frames
Unexpected ending and economy of text

tips: Change the camera distance (wide, close, high view) between frames.
Decide the ending first and work backwards.

title: The last day of a village well
prompt: A village hand pump replaces an old stone well where people have met for generations. Draw a three-frame comic showing the well on its last day, the villagers' reactions and one frame showing what the old well becomes. Use short speech or labels only where needed.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Narrative sequence and idea for the well's new life
Use of text only where necessary

tips: Show time passing with light or sky.
Let one object tell the emotion (a rope, a pot, a bucket).

title: Save the stepwell water
prompt: Design a poster for a school campaign titled 'Every Drop Counts' (or a better title of your own) to be put up near water taps. The poster should work for children aged 8 to 12 who may not read English well. Use one strong image, a big title and not more than 15 words in all. Use at most three colours.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Strength of the central image or concept
Layout, hierarchy and readability from a distance
Use of a limited colour palette
Message works for the target audience

tips: Squint at your poster: if the main idea disappears, simplify.
Draw the image first, then place the text around it.

title: Poster from a single shape
prompt: Make a poster for a school Diwali science fair using only a circle as the base shape for every element in the picture. Add the name of the fair and the date in a single line. Colour it with two colours plus black.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Imaginative use of circles to make the picture

tips: Overlap, nest and repeat circles to build rangoli, diyas, planets or faces.
Keep the lettering simple and at the same level as the picture.

title: The autorickshaw seat
prompt: Observe an autorickshaw passenger seat (or recall one) and list five problems faced by users such as a mother with a baby, an elderly person and a college student with a laptop. For two of the problems, sketch an improvement and describe in one line how it helps each user.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Quality and variety of the five observed problems
Two sketched improvements that are workable

tips: Name each user and what they carry.
Prefer cheap and simple fixes that a local fabricator could make.

title: The village bus stop
prompt: A rural bus stop has a tin roof, one bench and no signboard. List the people who use it through a day (at least four types) and what each needs. Then draw a simple plan or view of a redesigned stop with at least three features, each labelled with the user it serves.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Range of users identified, with their needs

tips: Think of morning, noon, evening and night.
Use materials that are available locally.

title: Describe the animal
prompt: Draw an imaginary animal that lives on a high-altitude cold desert like Ladakh using these clues: long soft wool, feet that do not sink into snow, ears that save body heat, and a way to carry water for days. Do not draw a real animal. Name it and add two labels.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: All four clues visible in the drawing

tips: Mix features of a few real animals but give it a clear overall silhouette.
Show size by drawing a person or a rock next to it.

title: The room that belongs to someone
prompt: Draw a corner of a room using these clues only: the owner is a left-handed cricket-loving grandmother who sews, wakes before dawn and keeps a pet parrot. Show at least six objects, with their positions telling the story of who lives there.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Composition and perspective of the corner

tips: Place objects in the way a person really uses them.
A single light source (a window) will help your shading.

title: Reinvent the steel tiffin
prompt: The three-tier steel tiffin carrier is still used by many office workers. Sketch a redesigned version for a student who also has to carry a water bottle and cutlery on a crowded local train. Show it in one view, one close-up of the latch or handle, and one line on what changed and why.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colour pencils or sketch pens, A4 sheet

rubric.criterion: Understanding of use on a crowded train
Design changes with a clear reason

tips: Keep what already works (stacking, steel, easy cleaning).
Draw the object in use at least once.

title: Is a single-use plastic ban enough?
prompt: Many Indian cities have restricted single-use plastic, yet roadside vendors still pack food in thin covers because alternatives cost more. In about 150 words, argue whether a ban alone is enough, and name who is affected most. Then sketch a design intervention (a product, a system or a service) that addresses one weakness in your argument and label it.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colours, A4 sheets (two)

rubric.criterion: Argument is balanced and supported with reasons
Identification of stakeholders (vendors, buyers, waste pickers, city)
Intervention addresses a weakness named in the argument

tips: State your position in the first sentence.
Use one real example from your own neighbourhood.
Make the sketch show how the intervention is used, not just its shape.

title: Digital payments and the elderly
prompt: UPI payments have changed small shopping, but many older people and small vendors with low literacy find the screens confusing. In about 150 words, analyse two barriers they face and what the designer should not assume. Then sketch an interface or physical aid that reduces one of those barriers.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colours, A4 sheets (two)

rubric.criterion: Depth of analysis of the two barriers
Practicality and inclusivity of the sketched solution

tips: Think in terms of vision, memory, trust and language.
Mention how you would test the idea with real users.

title: Heritage versus a new flyover
prompt: A narrow lane in an old city has a 200-year-old market. The city plans to widen the road, which will remove half of the shopfronts. Write a short argument (about 150 words) on how a designer might balance heritage, livelihoods and traffic. Then draw a section or plan of your proposed compromise.
materials: Pencil, eraser, colours, A4 sheets (two)

rubric.criterion: Recognition of competing needs and trade-offs
Spatial proposal is sensible and drawn clearly

tips: Name who gains and who loses in your solution.
Label dimensions roughly so the drawing is believable.

title: Eight cubes, one idea
prompt: Using 8 identical small paper or cardboard cubes (about 4 cm each, made by you) create a stable composition that expresses 'Growth'. All cubes must touch at least one other cube along a face or an edge. Photograph it from the front and from above and give it a title.
materials: Thin cardboard or chart paper, glue, scissors, ruler, pencil, phone camera

rubric.criterion: Rhythm, balance and use of space
Craft: accuracy of cubes and neat joints

tips: Make one cube template and copy it exactly.
Try three arrangements on a table before gluing.

title: Paper tower between two books
prompt: Build a free-standing structure using only 6 sheets of A4 paper and a little glue or tape. It must be at least 25 cm tall and hold a small plastic bottle cap (or a coin) at the top for 10 seconds. Draw a side view with labels afterwards.
materials: 6 A4 sheets, glue or tape, scissors, a coin, ruler
tips: Rolled tubes and triangulated frames are stronger than flat sheets.
Test the base first: a wide base helps.

title: Dialogue of two forms
prompt: Use two forms made of clay or dough: one smooth and round, one angular and sharp. Arrange them with a third small element (a leaf, a stick or a stone) so that the three seem to be in conversation. Keep the whole work within a 15 cm square base. Give it a title.
materials: Clay or dough, a stick or leaf, base card 15 cm square

rubric.criterion: Relationship and tension between the three elements

tips: Look at the work from all sides as you place elements.
Do not make the forms look like real objects; keep them abstract.

title: Mini shelter for a street dog
prompt: Make a working model (about 25 cm long) of a weatherproof shelter for a street dog during monsoon. It must stand on its own, have an entrance sized for a dog, and show how rain and heat are handled. Use only waste material. Add a labelled sketch of the idea.
materials: Waste cardboard, old plastic cover, newspaper, glue, tape, scissors, sketch sheet

rubric.criterion: Understanding of the user (dog) and the weather

tips: Slope the roof so water runs off and a lip keeps it off the entrance.
Use thin material cut accurately; avoid over-gluing.

title: A folding lamp shade
prompt: Design and make a model of a table lamp shade from one A3 sheet or equivalent, using cuts and folds only (no extra pieces). It must stand on its own, allow a gap for the bulb and cast an interesting pattern of light when a phone torch is placed under it. Photograph the shadow pattern.
materials: A3 sheet or chart paper, cutter or scissors, ruler, phone torch, glue optional
tips: Fold test with a small square of paper first.
Cut-outs in repeated patterns make strong shadows.

title: Moving toy with straws
prompt: Make a toy that moves when a straw is blown through, pushed or pulled, using straws, paper and thread. The idea may be a bird, a boat, a pedalling cyclist or anything you like. Show the moving part in two photos.
materials: Straws, thread, paper, card, glue, tape, scissors

rubric.criterion: Idea and character of the toy

tips: Plan the pivot or thread path before decorating.
Keep weight low so the toy moves easily.

title: Temple at sunrise and sunset
prompt: Make two small squares (10 cm each) of the same temple gopuram shape: one at sunrise, the other at dusk. The shape and layout must be identical; only colours change. Use a limited palette of five colours for each and name the mood of each.
materials: Colours (poster or pencil), 2 squares of paper 10 cm, pencil

rubric.criterion: Same drawing and layout in both

tips: Plan colours with a small swatch strip first.
Use warm and cool colours consciously.

title: Colour of a market
prompt: Paint a 15 cm x 15 cm abstract composition inspired by a vegetable market using only flat colour shapes (no outlines). Use colour proportions: one dominant colour (about 60 per cent), one supporting (30 per cent) and one accent (10 per cent). Add a small key of the three colours.
materials: Poster colours or crayons, paper, brush, pencil

rubric.criterion: Proportion of dominant, supporting and accent colour
Market feeling expressed in shapes and colours

tips: Squint to check the 60-30-10 ratio.
Place the accent where you want the eye to rest.

title: Monochrome to full colour
prompt: Make a composition of a single object (a lemon, a pot or a shoe) in four panels: pencil tones only; one hue with tints and shades; two complementary colours; free full colour. Use panels of 7 cm squares. Add one line about what each panel changed.
materials: Pencil, colours, paper, scale

rubric.criterion: Accuracy of object drawing across panels

tips: Draw the object once lightly and trace it for the other panels.
Add white or black for tints and shades; do not add other hues.

title: Texture collection board
prompt: Collect eight surfaces (leaf, bark, cloth, sandpaper, rangoli powder, foil, rope, newspaper) and make rubbings or small samples on one A4 board. Arrange them in a pleasing grid and then make one pattern inspired by any two of them. Label what each texture feels like in one word.
materials: Pencil, crayon, tracing or plain paper, glue, objects found at home
tips: Use the side of a pencil for rubbings.
Keep sample sizes equal.

title: Kolam-inspired repeat
prompt: Create a repeat pattern in a 12 cm square based on the logic of a kolam or rangoli dot grid, but use your own motif. The pattern must repeat in at least four directions and show symmetry. Fill with two colours. Draw the dot grid lightly first and do not erase the dots at the end.
materials: Pencil, scale, two colours, paper
tips: Design one quarter and mirror it.
Keep the lines continuous where the kolam tradition requires.

title: Pattern from a drawn texture
prompt: Draw the texture of a pineapple, a pebble or a leaf in pencil using only dots, lines and small marks, then change one mark type to create a new pattern with the same pattern idea. Make both on an A5 page side by side.
materials: Pencil, fine pen, A5 paper
tips: Squint to see big patches before adding small marks.
Use pressure variation to show depth.

title: Hands holding something
prompt: Observe your own non-drawing hand holding a steel tumbler, a book or a ball. Make a tonal pencil drawing on A4 showing proportion, overlapping and light and shade. Spend five minutes on a quick outline before the detailed one.
materials: Pencils (HB, 2B), eraser, A4 paper, the object

rubric.criterion: Proportion and shape of the hand

tips: Compare lengths of fingers by measuring with your pencil.
Draw the negative shapes between fingers.

title: Kitchen still life
prompt: Arrange three household objects of different shapes (for example a steel glass, an onion and a spoon) and draw the group from where you sit. Show the ground shadows and the relationship between sizes. Use only pencil. Add your viewpoint in a small diagram.
materials: Pencils, eraser, A4 paper, three objects, a lamp or window light
tips: Light from one side only.
Find the lightest and darkest areas first.

title: Crowd on a street
prompt: Make a 15-minute quick sketch of the street, balcony or courtyard view from your home or school. Fill the page with a foreground, middle ground and background; show at least five people or vehicles in small gestures. Do not rub any lines.
materials: Pencil or pen, A4 paper
tips: Use simple shapes for people.
Let near objects overlap far ones.

title: Redesign a comb
prompt: Take an ordinary plastic comb and, using card or clay, make a model of a redesigned comb for someone with limited hand strength (for example an elderly person with arthritis). Show the handle, the teeth spacing and the way it is gripped. Photograph it in the hand and add three annotations.
materials: Cardboard or clay, scissors, glue, an ordinary comb, camera
tips: Try different handle thicknesses on your own hand.
Test whether it can be held with a loose hand.
